title: Do Humans Have Hidden Regenerative Powers?
hook: Salamanders regrow lost limbs; mammals just scar over. New work hints our regenerative ability isn't gone — only switched off — and that it might be switched back on.
key_points: Mammals' ability to rebuild complex body parts may be switched off, not lost.
A two-stage treatment redirected the body's healing away from scarring and toward regrowth.
In animal studies, it restored bone, joints, ligaments, and tendons after amputation.
The work is early and done in animals — not yet a human therapy.
content_html: Some animals shrug off injuries we couldn't imagine recovering from — a salamander regrows a whole limb. Mammals, including us, mostly seal a wound with scar tissue and move on. New research suggests that gap may be smaller than it looks: the ability to rebuild complex body parts might not be lost in mammals, just switched off.
extra_html:
Using a two-stage treatment, ScienceDaily reports, researchers redirected the body's normal healing response away from scar formation and toward genuine regrowth. In animal studies, that was enough to restore bone, joints, ligaments, and tendons after amputation.

It's a striking proof of concept, but worth reading with care: this is early-stage work in animals, not a therapy people can get. The exciting idea isn't that humans will regrow limbs tomorrow — it's that regeneration may be a dormant capacity waiting for the right signal, rather than something evolution permanently took away.

flashcards.back_html: Mammals may not have lost the ability to regrow complex body parts — it may simply be switched off, raising the possibility it could be switched back on.

flashcards.prompt: What did the two-stage treatment achieve in animal studies?
